forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Wirral awarded up to £27.5m exceptional financial support for 2024/25 and 2025/26, and asks again for 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Wirral Council was awarded up to £27.5m of exceptional financial support (EFS, government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending) for 2024/25 and 2025/26, according to its external auditor's annual report for 2024/25, which went to the Audit and Risk Management Committee on 27 October 2026.

The auditor's report says the council could not balance its 2024/25 budget without government intervention. It used up to £20m of EFS that year, of which it utilised £18.6m. The report says this is the second time the council has been awarded EFS since 2021.

The council has since asked for EFS for the financial year 2026/27. A review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) was commissioned by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government following that request. The committee paper says the review was commissioned as a condition associated with the EFS and has no direct additional financial implications. It was carried out in April and May 2026.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Auditors Annual Report for Wirral Council 2024 2025

news_drafts.headline: Wirral schools funding deficit forecast to reach £120m by end of 2026/27, funded by borrowing
news_drafts.lead:
Wirral Council expects its schools funding deficit to reach £120m by the end of 2026/27 and is paying for it by borrowing. The figure is in the council's prudential indicators (the limits and measures every council must publish to show its borrowing is affordable), which go to full Council on 12 October. The deficit is an overspend on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, mainly on support for children with special educational needs.

The papers say the council is meeting the deficit through capital borrowing rather than from its day-to-day budget, and describe it as continuing to grow. As a result, its borrowing is above its capital financing requirement (CFR), the total it has spent on long-lived assets and not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow. At 31 March 2026 borrowing was £640.335m against a requirement of £565.087m. By 31 March 2029 it is estimated at £744.893m against £582.922m.

The government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant, payable in autumn 2026, equal to 90% of the deficit at the end of 2025/26, which stood at £66.410m. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special needs. The council says the grant "will not be sufficient to bring the Council's external debt back below its CFR", and expects borrowing to remain above the requirement at the end of 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: Merseyside Pension Fund audit unqualified pending £13.6m investment variance resolution
news_drafts.lead: Grant Thornton's audit of the Merseyside Pension Fund is anticipated to result in an unqualified opinion on its financial statements, subject to completion of outstanding work. However, auditors have identified a £13.6m difference between the fund's valuations of complex investments, known as Level 3 assets, and confirmations from external managers as at 31 March 2026. The fund's accounts, with net assets of £12,189m, do not adjust for this variance. Management asserts the difference is immaterial both quantitatively and qualitatively, sitting above the £7.3m reporting threshold but below performance materiality of £109.5m. Auditors are still awaiting three Level 3 investment confirmations from fund managers and one related party declaration before finalising their opinion. The audit fee is proposed at £128,262.
news_drafts.paper_title: 26Sept PB Audit Findings Report for MPF

findings.headline: The paper states that the Council's current Capital Programme does not contain schemes primarily focused on a commercial return.
findings.detail: The statement sits in the PWLB eligibility section, which says authorities planning to buy investment assets primarily for yield cannot access the PWLB except to refinance or externalise internal borrowing. The Section 151 Officer's confirmation of capital purpose is also required.
findings.matters: The PWLB eligibility condition depends on capital purpose, so a finance director or lender needs to know whether a council's programme meets it.
findings.quote: The Council’s current Capital Programme does not contain schemes that are primarily focussed on a commercial return.

findings.headline: The Market Loans (LOBO) balance was £43.50m at both 31 March and 30 September 2026, with no maturities or additions recorded.
findings.detail: The LOBO line shows no movement in the half-year. The paper does not mention call dates, lender rate proposals, or any change to these loans.
findings.matters: LOBO stock with lender call options is a specific risk that lenders and finance directors at other councils track closely, so the unchanged balance is the fact to note.
findings.figures: £43.50m LOBO balance at 31 March 2026; £43.50m at 30 September 2026; £0.00m maturities and additions

findings.headline: Temporary cashflow loans of £349.00m matured and £347.00m were drawn in the half-year, reducing the balance from £65.00m to £63.00m.
findings.detail: Table B1 shows the temporary cashflow line rolled over during the period, with almost the same value drawn as matured. The net movement was a £2.0m reduction.
findings.matters: A high turnover of short-term loans shows how much funding must be replaced within a single half-year, which is relevant to refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £65.00m opening balance; £349.00m maturities; £347.00m additions; £63.00m closing balance; £2.0m net reduction

findings.headline: The Council held £63m of short-term local council loans at 30 September 2026, at an average rate of 4.28%.
findings.detail: The paper describes use of the short-term local council loan market as a source of borrowing when cashflow requires it. The £63m is the temporary cashflow balance shown in Table B1.
findings.matters: The size of the short-term balance and its average rate show how far the Council relies on rolling short-term funding, which a lender or peer would weigh against long-term borrowing.
findings.quote: the Council had £63 million borrowed via such loans running at an average rate of 4.28%.

findings.headline: The Council arranged a new £10m PWLB loan at 5.28%, with the final instalment due on 23/09/2028.
findings.detail: Table B3 records one PWLB loan arranged since 31 March 2026, repayable in equal instalments of principal. The repayments in Table B2 carried rates from 2.160% to 5.350%, with most between 4.3% and 5.3%.
findings.matters: A new drawdown rate set against the rates on the loans being repaid shows the Council's replacement cost, which is useful to peers and lenders pricing similar councils.
findings.figures: £10m new PWLB borrowing; 5.28% rate; 23/09/2028 loan maturity; repaid PWLB rates from 2.160% to 5.350%

daily_post.headline: Quarter 1 monitoring report to Policy & Resources on 22 July 2026 included the headline forecast DSG deficit and its treasury management impact
daily_post.lead: A council's DSG deficit and the treasury management cost of carrying it are central to how other councils and lenders assess the position of high-needs budgets.
